passage:
I'm Alka. Last Diwali my cousin Anjali, sixteen, cornered me on the terrace. "Didi, you're an engineer. Should I do engineering too? Papa says yes."

My first instinct was to give her my whole plan. Science, coaching, the entrance exam, the same college I went to. It had worked for me.

But something made me stop. I remembered how miserable I'd been in my second year, wondering if I'd chosen for myself or for my parents.

So I asked, "What do you actually enjoy?"

She thought for a long time. "Biology. Animals. Is that stupid?"

"Not at all." I told her honestly what engineering was like, the good and the boring. Then I said I didn't know much about biology careers, but my college friend was a wildlife researcher. I gave Anjali her number.

They've talked twice since. Anjali's choosing biology. Papa grumbled. I told him it's her path, not mine.

qa.q: What subject did Anjali say she enjoys?
qa.a: Biology, and animals.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling when her first instinct was to give Anjali her whole plan?
qa.a: She felt eager to help but then uneasy, remembering how miserable she'd been wondering whether she had chosen for herself.

qa.q: What did Alka do well as a guide for Anjali?
qa.a: She asked what Anjali enjoyed, shared her own experience honestly, admitted what she didn't know, and connected Anjali to a wildlife researcher.

qa.q: How might Anjali's Papa see Alka's role?
qa.a: Papa may be a bit annoyed, having wanted Anjali to do engineering, and may feel Alka encouraged a different path.

grounding: The reflective account shows a young woman guiding a younger cousin about careers with humility, listening to what she wants and connecting her to resources rather than pushing her own path.

passage:
Career counsellor's note, Class 12 guidance day

Irawati came to today's session with her older sister, Alka, who works as a chartered accountant in Pune. I watched them for most of the hour.

Irawati said she was interested in design. I noticed Alka start to say something, probably about commerce, then stop. Instead Alka asked, "What kind of design? What do you like making?"

Irawati talked about posters she makes for her school events. Alka listened and asked good questions. When Irawati asked what Alka's own job was like, Alka answered honestly: steady, often dull, and not for everyone.

Alka then asked me which design colleges we had information on, and took all the brochures. She suggested Irawati talk to a designer friend of hers before deciding.

It was good to see an older sibling who listened more than advised.

Next step: I'm sending both sisters the dates of the design entrance workshops.

Career counsellor

qa.q: What does Irawati make for her school events?
qa.a: Posters.

qa.q: What does Alka's pause before speaking suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Alka was tempted to push commerce but held back, wanting to listen rather than impose her own path.

qa.q: What did Alka do that helped Irawati?
qa.a: Alka asked what Irawati liked making, answered honestly about accounting, collected design college brochures, and suggested talking to a designer friend.

qa.q: How might Irawati see her sister's support?
qa.a: Irawati likely felt listened to and encouraged, rather than pushed into commerce.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows an older sister guiding a younger one about careers, listening more than advising, sharing her own experience honestly and connecting her to resources.

passage:
Rehana's diary. Friday.

It's been six years, and I still think about what I did to Irfan in college. I started a rumour that he'd cheated in the mid-term. I was jealous of his marks. It spread. People stopped sitting with him. He left the hostel mid-year.

I've replayed it hundreds of times. I've called myself every name.

Today, finally, I stopped just replaying it. I found Irfan online and wrote to him. I said exactly what I did, that it was a lie, that I was jealous, and that I was sorry for the months it cost him. I didn't ask him to forgive me. I offered to write to our old professor to clear his name, if he wanted.

He hasn't replied. He might never. That's his right.

But I'm going to stop punishing myself every night. I've owned it. I've tried to repair it. What I can do now is never do it to anyone again. That, I can promise.

qa.q: What rumour did Rehana start about Irfan?
qa.a: That he had cheated in the mid-term.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling in the years after the rumour?
qa.a: Rehana felt deep guilt and shame, replaying it hundreds of times with harsh self-blame.

qa.q: What steps did Rehana take to repair the harm?
qa.a: Rehana wrote to Irfan admitting exactly what happened and why, apologised without asking for forgiveness, and offered to clear his name with their old professor.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel receiving Rehana's message?
qa.a: Irfan may feel a mix of old anger and some relief that the truth was finally admitted, and may need time before replying.

grounding: The diary shows someone still haunted by a harmful mistake from years ago, owning it, making amends where possible, and choosing to move on through changed behaviour.

passage:
Jaya came home to the village near Nashik for the harvest, the first time in two years. Her mother was bent over the onion field, as she had been every day of Jaya's childhood.

Growing up, Jaya had resented her. Amma never came to school functions. She shouted when Jaya asked for money for books. She never said "well done."

That evening, sorting onions on the veranda, Jaya's brother Sahil said quietly, "You know she was sixteen when she married. Papa drank. She ran the field alone."

Jaya's hands stopped. She'd known, but she'd never put it together.

She watched her mother's cracked hands, tying bundles. At twenty-five, Jaya earned a salary in Pune and had never once had to choose between food and books.

Something in her loosened. It didn't make the shouting right. But she understood where it came from.

"Amma," she said. "Let me do that. You sit."

Her mother looked at her, surprised, and sat.

qa.q: How old was Amma when she married, according to Sahil?
qa.a: Sixteen.

qa.q: What did Jaya feel as she watched her mother's cracked hands?
qa.a: Her resentment loosened into understanding and tenderness, though she still felt the old hurt.

qa.q: How does Jaya's response balance forgiveness and honesty?
qa.a: She releases her resentment and helps her mother, without pretending the shouting was right.

qa.q: How might Amma see Jaya's offer to take over?
qa.a: Amma seems surprised and perhaps touched, since she has rarely been cared for this way.

grounding: The passage shows a young woman understanding her mother's hard life and limits, releasing resentment without excusing harm, and appreciating the effort she made.

passage:
Two years ago, Bidisha had told the whole cooperative in their town near Bardhaman that Darshan was stealing from the milk collection. It was a lie. He had been cleared, but half the village still looked at him sideways.

For months Darshan had imagined saying something cruel back. Posting her secrets. Making her feel it.

Now Bidisha had moved back, and he saw her at the bus stand. His stomach clenched.

That night he talked to his grandfather. "I can't stop being angry."

"Anger is a hot coal in your own hand," the old man said. "You don't have to be friends with her. Just put it down."

Darshan thought about it for a week. He didn't seek her out. He didn't plan revenge. When they passed at the market, he nodded politely and walked on.

A month later, Bidisha came to his door. "I was wrong. I'm sorry." He listened. He said he accepted it. He did not invite her in.

qa.q: What lie had Bidisha told about Darshan?
qa.a: That he was stealing from the milk collection.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling when he saw Bidisha at the bus stand?
qa.a: He felt tense and angry, his stomach clenching, with old revenge fantasies close to the surface.

qa.q: How did Darshan's forgiveness protect his own peace?
qa.a: He let go of revenge, kept a polite distance, and accepted her apology without restoring closeness or trust.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt coming to Darshan's door?
qa.a: Bidisha may have felt ashamed and nervous, finally admitting she was wrong.

grounding: The passage shows someone badly hurt by a former friend's lie letting go of revenge for his own peace, keeping a safe distance, and accepting a real apology without reconciling.

passage:
Daniel and Siddiq had shared a flat in Toronto for three years. Then Siddiq left overnight with two months of unpaid rent and Daniel's bicycle, and blocked his number.

For a year, Daniel imagined running into him. He rehearsed speeches. He checked Siddiq's profile late at night.

His sister finally said, "You're letting him live in your head rent-free, too."

That landed. Daniel stopped checking. He blocked Siddiq's profile himself. When friends brought him up, Daniel changed the subject.

Eighteen months later, an email arrived. Siddiq wrote that he'd been in debt and ashamed, that he'd been wrong, and he offered to return the bicycle.

Daniel read it three times. It named what Siddiq had done. It didn't make excuses.

He replied: "Thank you for saying it. I accept your apology. I'd like the bike back. I don't think we'll be close again, but I wish you well."

Then he closed the laptop and went for a run, feeling lighter.

qa.q: What did Siddiq offer to return?
qa.a: Daniel's bicycle.

qa.q: What was Daniel feeling as he checked Siddiq's profile at night?
qa.a: He felt resentful and stuck, replaying speeches and unable to let go of the hurt.

qa.q: What did Daniel do that helped him find peace?
qa.a: He stopped checking Siddiq's profile, let go of revenge speeches, and later accepted a real apology while keeping his distance.

qa.q: How might Siddiq have felt writing the email?
qa.a: Siddiq may have felt ashamed and nervous, hoping to make some amends for what he did.

grounding: The passage shows someone badly hurt by a former friend forgiving for his own peace, dropping revenge fantasies, keeping distance and accepting a real apology without full reconciliation.

passage:
Dear Jeevan,

Thank you for your message, even though it was hard to read. You're right to be angry.

Two years ago, when we built the inventory tool together, I presented it to the directors as mine. I didn't mention your name. I got the promotion. You got nothing, and you left the company a few months later.

I'm not going to explain why. There's no good reason. I was scared of being ordinary, and I took something that was yours.

I'm sorry for taking credit for your work, for staying silent when you asked about it, and for the months of doubt it caused you.

I don't expect forgiveness. If you ever want me to, I'll write to the directors and tell them the truth about who built it. I'll also give a reference to anyone you want.

Whether you reply or not is up to you. I'll respect either.

Mehak

qa.q: What did Mehak present to the directors as Mehak's own?
qa.a: The inventory tool Mehak and Jeevan built together.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling while writing to Jeevan?
qa.a: Mehak felt guilty and ashamed about taking credit, and ready to face Jeevan's anger without making excuses.

qa.q: What did Mehak do right in the apology?
qa.a: Mehak listened to Jeevan's anger, named exactly what happened without excuses, didn't demand forgiveness, and offered concrete repair like telling the directors the truth.

grounding: The letter shows someone who wronged an old colleague responding to that anger by listening, apologising specifically, offering repair and leaving forgiveness to Jeevan.

passage:
"So I got this message from Swati last month. I'm Pranav, by the way, and this is the most embarrassing story I have.

Three years ago, we were close. Like, planning-a-trip close. Then I just stopped replying. No explanation. I was going through a bad patch and it was easier to disappear than to explain.

Her message was angry. 'You made me feel like I was nothing. I thought I'd done something wrong for a year.'

My first reflex was to defend myself. I was depressed, I was busy, whatever. I typed it and deleted it.

Instead I wrote, 'You're right. I disappeared without a word, and it wasn't anything you did. I'm really sorry for making you doubt yourself for so long.'

I didn't ask her to forgive me. I said if she ever wanted to talk it through, I'd listen.

She replied two weeks later. Just: 'Thanks for not making excuses.' That's all. And honestly, that's enough."

passage:
Seema was stuck in a jam on the Bengaluru ring road, forty minutes and counting, and her mind went where it always went: to Jatin, her old manager.

Two years ago, in front of the whole team, he'd called her report "school-level rubbish." She'd left that job. She had a better one now. But in every traffic jam, every quiet moment, she replayed it and wrote sharp replies in her head.

Today, her car inched forward and she noticed her jaw aching. She had been clenching it for twenty minutes.

That evening she told her flatmate, who listened and then asked, "What do you actually want from him?"

Seema thought. "An apology. But he'll never give one."

"So what do you need, if he never does?"

It took a few weeks and two sessions with a counsellor. She wrote Jatin a letter she never sent, listing every word he'd said. Then she tore it up. The next jam, she put on music instead.

qa.q: What did Jatin call Seema's report?
qa.a: "School-level rubbish."

qa.q: What was Seema feeling as she noticed her jaw aching?
qa.a: She felt a tight, lingering resentment, still replaying the old insult two years later.

qa.q: What did Seema do to free herself from the resentment?

At every family function in Lucknow, Zainab found herself watching her cousin Eshaan across the room and remembering.

At her engagement three years ago, he had loudly said her fiancé was "marrying down." Everyone had laughed. The engagement was long over now, for other reasons, but the laugh stayed.

At tonight's Eid dinner, Eshaan waved at her. She pretended not to see. Her chest felt hot all evening, and she barely tasted the biryani.

On the drive home, her friend asked why she'd been so quiet.

"I keep carrying this thing he said. It's like holding a hot stone, waiting to throw it back."

"And he doesn't even know you're holding it," her friend said.

Zainab laughed despite herself. Then she thought: what did she actually need? Not revenge. Maybe just not to give him her evenings.

The next time Eshaan waved, she waved back briefly and went to find her grandmother. It was a small thing. It felt like putting the stone down.

qa.q: What did Eshaan say at Zainab's engagement?
qa.a: That her fiancé was "marrying down."

passage:
Jamal hadn't spoken to Daniel in eight months, not since Daniel had mocked his stammer in front of their whole football team in Manchester.

On Saturday Daniel turned up at the pitch early. "Can I talk to you?"

Jamal folded his arms.

"What I said about your stammer was cruel," Daniel said. "I did it to look funny in front of the lads. I'm sorry. I've told the team it was out of order."

Jamal felt his throat tighten. It named exactly what happened. That counted for something.

"Why now?"

"My little brother started stammering. Kids at school laugh at him. I saw what I did."

Jamal nodded slowly. "Thanks for saying it. I accept that. But I'm not ready to be mates like before."

"That's fair."

Over the next few weeks, Jamal noticed Daniel shutting down other lads' jokes on the pitch. He still kept a little distance. But he started passing to him again.

qa.q: What had Daniel mocked in front of the team?
qa.a: Jamal's stammer.

qa.q: What was Jamal feeling when Daniel apologised?
qa.a: He felt moved and a bit wary, his throat tightening because the apology named exactly what happened.

qa.q: How did Jamal handle the apology wisely?
qa.a: He accepted it but didn't restore full trust at once, and watched whether Daniel's behaviour really changed before getting closer.

qa.q: Why might Daniel have finally apologised?
qa.a: Seeing his little brother laughed at for stammering made Daniel feel ashamed of what he had done to Jamal.

grounding: The passage shows someone hurt receiving a sincere apology that names the harm, accepting it without restoring full trust, and watching for changed behaviour.

passage:
In the hospital pharmacy in Coimbatore, Manjula was restocking shelves when Karthik came in with two cups of tea.

Last month, he had blamed her in front of the pharmacy head for a dispensing error that was actually his. She had nearly received a written warning.

"Manjula, I need to say something." He set the tea down. "The error on the 12th was mine. I blamed you because I was scared. I've told the pharmacy head the truth this morning. I'm sorry."

Manjula didn't pick up the tea. She'd lost sleep over that warning.

"You told her?"

"In writing. She's removing the note from your file."

It named what he did. He'd fixed the record. That mattered.

"Thank you," she said slowly. "I accept the apology. But I'll need time before I trust you on shift again."

"I understand."

That week she double-checked his entries. By the next month, she was checking a little less.

qa.q: When did the dispensing error happen?
qa.a: On the 12th.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when Karthik offered the tea?
qa.a: She felt wary and still hurt, having lost sleep over the warning he caused.

qa.q: What made Karthik's apology believable?
qa.a: He named exactly what he did, why, and fixed the record in writing with the pharmacy head.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel about Manjula needing time?

grounding: The passage shows someone receiving a sincere apology that names the harm and repairs it, accepting it while taking time before restoring full trust.

passage:
"Hansa, you've won the state chess title, well done. Now sit, and let me tell you about my biggest mistake.

When I, Bhupen, was twenty-four, I won the national quiz championship. My picture was in the paper. Everyone in Guwahati knew my name. For a year, every person I met told me I was brilliant.

And I believed them. I stopped studying properly. When my old coach pointed out that I'd been lucky in the final round, I laughed at him. I thought critics were just jealous.

The next year I lost in the first round to a seventeen-year-old from Silchar. I sat in the hall, humiliated.

Afterwards, I went to my coach and apologised. I thanked him for all those evenings he spent with me, unpaid. I asked him to show me what I'd got wrong.

Enjoy your win, beta. Then thank your teachers, and keep listening to the ones who tell you where you slipped."

Then Jomon, his co-founder, texted: "Great speech. Did you mention Ms. Mathew?"

Vikas stopped. Ms. Mathew, his college professor, had given them lab space for free for a year. He hadn't mentioned her. He hadn't mentioned the three interns either, or the lucky timing of the government scheme.

At the dinner, an older investor gently criticised their pricing model. Vikas's first instinct was to defend it.

He caught himself. "Tell me more. What are we missing?"

The investor talked for twenty minutes. Vikas took notes.

Before dessert, he stood up and thanked Ms. Mathew, the interns and Jomon by name.

passage:
The women's self-help group in the village near Siliguri had just won the district award for their mango pickle. The collector called Bhavna, the group leader, onto the stage.

She looked at the crowd. The trophy felt heavy. It would be so easy to just say thank you and sit.

Instead she said, "This isn't mine. Dolma-di found the old recipe from her grandmother. Rinku did all the accounts at night after her field work. Kamala-mashi carried the jars to the market on the bus every Thursday."

She called each of them up. They came, shy and laughing.

Later, when the district officer asked who should go to the state meeting in Kolkata, Bhavna said, "Send Dolma-di. It was her recipe."

The prize money was shared equally among all twelve women. On the bus home, Dolma held the trophy on her lap the whole way.

qa.q: Who found the old pickle recipe?
qa.a: Dolma-di, from her grandmother.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling as she held the trophy on stage?

qa.q: How did Bhavna share the credit, and why does it matter?

qa.q: How might Dolma feel holding the trophy on the bus?
qa.a: Dolma likely feels proud and valued, recognised for her grandmother's recipe.

passage:
Bao's software team in Ho Chi Minh City had just launched the new payments app on time, the first on-time launch the company had ever had. The regional director flew in to congratulate him.

"Your leadership made this happen," she said at the all-hands meeting.

Bao felt the glow of it. Then he looked at the back row, where Pablo, the Spanish engineer who had rewritten the whole checkout system over two sleepless weeks, was quietly eating a sandwich.

Bao stood up. "Thank you. But I want to be specific. Pablo rebuilt the checkout, and that's why we launched on time. Linh fixed the security gaps. Duc tested every screen at 2 a.m."

After the meeting, he emailed the regional director a short list of each person's contributions. He asked that the launch bonus be shared equally.

Pablo stopped by his desk later. "Nobody's ever done that before," he said. Bao just nodded, embarrassed.

qa.q: What system did Pablo rewrite?
qa.a: The whole checkout system.

qa.q: What did Bao feel when he looked at Pablo in the back row?
qa.a: He felt proud at first, then grateful and a little uneasy, sensing the credit belonged to Pablo and the others too.

qa.q: What did Bao do to share credit?
qa.a: He named Pablo, Linh and Duc publicly, emailed the director their contributions, and asked for the bonus to be shared equally.

grounding: The passage shows a team leader recognising that success was built by others, thanking them by name, sharing rewards and mentioning their contributions to senior leaders.

passage:
I'm Tejas. When I got the promotion to team lead last year, Lalremsiami was the first to text: "Congrats, boss!" with a row of party emojis.

But over the next few weeks, something shifted. At lunch she'd say, "Oh, sorry, sir, I'll let you speak first." Everyone laughed. When I mentioned the new laptop, she said, "Must be nice."

It stung. We'd started at the company on the same day, eaten the same bad canteen food for three years.

My first instinct was to pull rank or pull away. Instead I stopped mentioning anything new: the laptop, the meetings with directors. I kept going to our Friday momo place, same table, same order. I didn't push her to talk.

A month later, she got a big client win. I made sure the director heard about it, and I bought the momos.

She laughed properly that day. "Okay," she said. "You're still you."

Cricket coach's note, Sunday veterans' nets

Abhinav and Asif have opened the batting together for our club since they were fifteen. This season, Abhinav got selected for the state corporate team. Today was his first week back at our nets since.

I noticed Asif greet him with "Oh, the star has arrived!" loud enough for everyone. Twice more he made jokes: "Careful, don't bowl too fast at the famous man." Abhinav's smile looked tight.

Abhinav handled it well. He didn't talk about the state team at all. He asked Asif about his daughter's school admission. At the break he brought out the same flask of cutting chai they've shared since school days.

Later I heard Abhinav quietly tell Asif, "Your cover drive's better than mine. Always has been." Asif looked away, but I saw him smile.

Next step: I've put them back as openers for next Sunday's friendly, and asked Abhinav to help coach the juniors with Asif.

Coach
